BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- Preliminary DNA tests indicate a 3-year-old foster child is the son of a woman being held captive by leftist rebels, Colombian officials announced Friday. Clara Rojas appears in a video released by the kidnappers in July 2002. "There is a very high probability that Juan David belongs to the family of Clara Gonzalez de Rojas," Mario Iguaran Arana, the country's chief federal prosecutor, said at a news conference. The boy, known as "Emmanuel," has been at the center of a hostage drama that raised hopes the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia would liberate some of their hostages. The rebel group, known as FARC for its Spanish acronym, had agreed to release three hostages as part of a deal brokered by Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez. FARC said it would release Emmanuel along with his mother, Clara Rojas, and another woman, Consuelo Gonzalez, but the mission to free the captives fell apart December 31, when the rebel group said it could not release the hostages because of Colombian military operations in the area, according to a FARC statement Chavez read on Venezuelan television. Colombian President Alvaro Uribe denied the group's assertion, saying there were no combat operations in the area near the rebels, and he said the rebels could not release the three hostages because they did not have Emmanuel in custody. He raised the possibility that Emmanuel, who was born in captivity to Rojas, was living in a foster home in the Colombian capital of Bogota. Authorities in Colombia suspect the FARC duped child-welfare authorities by presenting the boy as a child in need of foster care in 2005, he said. On Friday, Iguaran Arana said initial DNA results will be checked against tests being done in European labs to verify the child's identity. There was no immediate response from Venezuela after the announcement concerning Emmanuel's DNA. However, a statement on the Venezuelan government's Web site from earlier Friday said the Colombian government had not allowed Venezuela to participate in the DNA testing. Established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party, FARC is Colombia's oldest, largest, most capable and best-equipped Marxist rebel group, according to the U.S. Department of State. The United States, the European Union and Colombia classify it as a terrorist group. FARC has justified hostage-taking as a legitimate military tactic in a long-running and complex civil war that also has involved right-wing paramilitary units, government forces and drug traffickers. Fighting has waned, but not stopped, in recent years. Among the group's hostages are three American contractors who were captured when their plane went down in 2003 during a drug-eradication flight, and Ingrid Betancourt, a French-Colombian independent presidential candidate who was kidnapped in 2002. Rojas was kidnapped in 2002 while she managed Betancourt's campaign. Betancourt is perhaps the best-known captive in Colombia, a country plagued by kidnapping.  E-mail to a friend .

**BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN-style wire story)** — A highly anticipated hostage release by Colombia’s largest rebel group collapsed Monday after guerrillas failed to turn over three captives, including a boy believed to have been born in captivity to a kidnapped politician, officials said.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, had pledged to release former vice presidential candidate Clara Rojas, former congresswoman Consuelo González de Perdomo and Rojas’ young son, Emmanuel, as part of a humanitarian gesture brokered with the help of Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez.

But the December 31 handover did not take place, and the failure deepened confusion over the whereabouts of Emmanuel, a child whose case has come to symbolize the suffering of hundreds of hostages held for years in Colombia’s jungle conflict.

Colombian President Álvaro Uribe said Monday that authorities believed Emmanuel was no longer in rebel hands and may have been living under government protection with the name Juan David.

“The FARC did not release the child because they do not have him,” Uribe said, accusing the rebels of misleading international mediators.

The FARC said in a statement that military operations in the area had prevented the release. Colombian officials rejected that explanation, saying the government had suspended operations in the proposed zone to allow an international mission to collect the hostages.

The failed handover was a setback for Chávez, who had arranged for aircraft, medical teams and international observers to travel into Colombia for the expected release. Representatives from several Latin American countries had joined the mission, which was halted after the rebels failed to provide coordinates for the pickup.

Rojas was kidnapped in 2002 while campaigning with Ingrid Betancourt, a presidential candidate who also remained in FARC captivity. During her captivity, Rojas gave birth to Emmanuel, reportedly fathered by a guerrilla fighter.

Colombian authorities said a child matching Emmanuel’s profile had been taken from the jungle years earlier by a man claiming to be a peasant and placed in state care after showing signs of poor health. The boy was later identified as Juan David. Officials said DNA tests were being used to confirm whether he was Rojas’ son.

The FARC, a Marxist guerrilla movement founded in the 1960s, has long used kidnapping as a political and financial tool. The group has held politicians, soldiers, police officers and civilians, demanding prisoner exchanges and concessions from the Colombian government.

Families of the hostages said the botched release had raised hopes only to crush them again.

The episode also intensified the political confrontation between Uribe and Chávez, who had been removed weeks earlier as an official mediator by the Colombian government but continued to press for a rebel handover.

Despite Monday’s failure, Colombian officials said they remained willing to facilitate a release if the FARC provided credible information.

“The country wants these people home,” a government spokesman said. “But Colombia will not accept manipulation over the life of a child.”

counterfactuals.output:
The Colombian government announced that a young boy living under state protection in Bogotá may be the son of **Clara Rojas**, a former vice-presidential candidate who had been held captive for years by the rebel group **FARC**.

Officials said the child, believed to be named **Emmanuel**, matched accounts of the boy reportedly born to Rojas while she was in guerrilla captivity. The government said it had located the child in a foster-care or child-welfare setting and was conducting DNA tests to confirm his identity.

## Key details of the announcement

Colombian authorities said the boy had been taken into the care of the state child-protection agency after being found in poor health and under unclear circumstances. Government officials suggested that FARC may have secretly removed the child from the jungle and placed him with civilians, rather than keeping him with his mother.

The claim was significant because FARC had recently promised to release **Clara Rojas**, former congresswoman **Consuelo González**, and Rojas’s son Emmanuel as part of a high-profile humanitarian gesture. If the government’s finding was correct, it meant FARC no longer had the child in its custody despite claiming he would be handed over.

President **Álvaro Uribe’s** administration said the discovery raised questions about the rebels’ credibility and their handling of hostages. The government argued that FARC’s announcement of a release had been complicated by the fact that Emmanuel was apparently already outside rebel control.

## Who is Clara Rojas?

Clara Rojas was the running mate of Colombian presidential candidate **Íngrid Betancourt** in the 2002 election. Both women were kidnapped by FARC in February 2002 while campaigning in a rebel-influenced region of southern Colombia.

During her captivity, Rojas reportedly gave birth to a son, Emmanuel. The child’s father was said to be a guerrilla fighter, though details were limited and came largely from accounts of former hostages and government intelligence.

Rojas became one of the most internationally recognized hostages held by FARC, partly because of her connection to Betancourt and partly because of the story of her child being born in captivity.

## Background on FARC

The **Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia**, known by its Spanish acronym **FARC**, was Colombia’s largest leftist guerrilla organization. Founded in the 1960s, it grew out of rural Marxist insurgent movements and claimed to fight for land reform and social justice.

Over decades, FARC funded itself through kidnapping, extortion, illegal mining, and involvement in the cocaine trade. The group became notorious for holding soldiers, police, politicians, and civilians in jungle camps for years, often seeking prisoner exchanges or political concessions.

By the 2000s, FARC was under heavy military pressure from the Colombian state, especially under President Uribe, whose security policies were backed by U.S. assistance through **Plan Colombia**. Even so, the rebels continued to hold high-profile captives.

## Other prominent hostages

Among the most famous FARC captives was **Íngrid Betancourt**, a dual Colombian-French citizen whose kidnapping drew international attention, particularly from France and human-rights groups. Betancourt’s case became a symbol of the wider hostage crisis in Colombia.

FARC also held numerous Colombian soldiers and police officers, some for a decade or more. The guerrillas sought to exchange them for imprisoned rebels. Families of hostages often campaigned publicly for a negotiated humanitarian swap, while the Uribe government resisted concessions it believed would strengthen FARC.

Former congresswoman **Consuelo González** was another political hostage whom FARC had said it would release. Her expected release, along with Rojas and Emmanuel, was tied to mediation efforts involving Venezuelan President **Hugo Chávez**, who had been trying to broker a humanitarian exchange before tensions with Bogotá disrupted the process.

## Why the discovery mattered

The possible identification of Emmanuel in state custody reshaped the planned hostage release. If DNA tests confirmed the child was Rojas’s son, it would show that FARC had misrepresented its ability to deliver all three promised hostages.

It also highlighted the harsh conditions faced by captives and their families, particularly children born or raised in conflict zones. For the Colombian government, the case became both a humanitarian issue and a political blow against FARC’s public image.

For relatives of hostages, however, the announcement was another painful reminder of the uncertainty surrounding those still held in the jungle and the difficulty of securing their freedom.

Iguaran said forensic testing verified that one of the bodies recovered after the cross-border raid was that of Raúl Reyes, a top FARC commander and longtime spokesman for the rebel group. Reyes was killed when Colombian forces attacked a guerrilla camp just inside Ecuador, an operation that sparked a diplomatic crisis between Colombia and its neighbors.

Uribe’s government has defended the raid as a necessary strike against a rebel organization it says has carried out kidnappings, bombings and drug trafficking for decades. Colombian officials also say computers and documents seized at the camp show links between the FARC and foreign governments, including Venezuela.

Uribe has claimed that the material recovered from the site suggests the FARC sought international support, discussed weapons and funding, and maintained contacts with officials outside Colombia. Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez has denied supporting the guerrillas and has accused Uribe of using the raid to provoke a wider regional conflict.

The Colombian president has repeatedly alleged that Venezuela has offered political or logistical backing to the FARC, a charge Caracas rejects. Venezuela, in turn, has condemned Colombia’s incursion into Ecuadorian territory as a violation of sovereignty. Ecuador also broke diplomatic ties with Colombia after the operation, saying Bogota failed to obtain permission before launching the attack.

The dispute has drawn international concern because it involves three countries already divided over security policy and relations with the United States. Colombia is Washington’s closest ally in the region and has received billions of dollars in U.S. military and anti-narcotics assistance. Venezuela, under Chávez, has positioned itself as a leading critic of U.S. influence in Latin America.

The FARC, founded in the 1960s as a Marxist insurgency, is Latin America’s oldest active rebel movement. It began as a peasant-based guerrilla force but grew into a powerful armed group funded in large part through kidnapping, extortion and the cocaine trade, according to Colombian and U.S. officials. The United States and European Union have designated the FARC as a terrorist organization.

For decades, the rebels have fought Colombian security forces while controlling rural strongholds, especially in jungle and mountain regions. The conflict has displaced millions of Colombians and claimed tens of thousands of lives, involving not only guerrillas but also right-wing paramilitary groups, drug cartels and government forces.

Reyes had been one of the FARC’s most visible leaders, often serving as a public voice for the group in negotiations and communications with foreign intermediaries. His death was considered one of the most significant blows to the rebel leadership in years.

Colombian officials say the DNA confirmation strengthens their case that the raid struck a major FARC command center. But the diplomatic fallout remains unresolved, with Venezuela and Ecuador demanding accountability and Colombia insisting it acted in self-defense against a group operating beyond its borders.
